prize_parts.citation: For developing the political-economy theory of trade policy, showing how lobbying and special-interest politics shape trade protection.

statement.case_for: My laureates and ballot are unchanged from round 1: a single part on B001 for Helpman and Grossman. What has changed is how tightly I would draw the citation. The protection-for-sale framework made lobbying and tariff formation a tractable general-equilibrium object with sharp, falsifiable cross-sector predictions. It has organised theory, estimation and the analysis of trade agreements for about thirty years. The credit is two people with a tightly coupled joint programme, so no one needs to be arbitrarily excluded and there are no unresolved gaps like those in the other leading candidates. Maturity is not in question. The round-1 exchange sharpened the framing issue. I now think the citation should rest only on the political economy of trade policy, which is the discovery the ballot defines. The innovation-growth-trade strand is genuine joint work, but putting it in the citation would invite the overlap question with the 2025 prize (as reported in the files, not verified by me) and would blur the credit. The case rests on conceptual generality, durable influence, clean attribution and maturity. It does not rest on how many colleagues prefer B001, and I treat the chair's summary of support as a process record, not evidence.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is still empirical. Support for the specific protection-for-sale predictions is mixed and sensitive to specification and setting, so part of the contribution is an organising framework and research programme, not a settled quantitative result. A prize committee could reasonably want a tested finding. A second concern is distinctness from Krugman's 2008 prize and from the 2025 growth prize, which I cannot verify beyond what colleagues report. A third is that Helpman is also credited on B030. A committee that prefers to honour trade through firm heterogeneity would face a different choice, and I accept that B030 is not a weaker contribution on importance. Finally, I do not rest my view on a belief that the empirical record is favourable. It is mixed, and the citation should say so by not claiming validation.

responses.point: Krusell finds the mixed empirical record of protection-for-sale more worrying than the B001 supporters do. He reads it as a sign that the lasting value is an organising theory, whereas BLP has been validated by three decades of practice. He now calls B001 a close alternative to B002 and says the two differ in kind, method versus theoretical framework.
responses.response: This is the sharpest version of the empirical objection and I take it seriously. Practical validation is a real strength of B002, and I do not dismiss it. I would put the standard differently, though. A theory should be judged on whether it made a previously vague question precisely answerable and whether it generated a research programme that could confirm or refute it. Protection-for-sale did that, and the mixed results come from that testability. I also stay with my round-1 position that the BLP triple leaves out Bresnahan and Reiss, and that Pakes's dynamic-games work is partly a separate strand. That makes the credit boundary of B002 less clean than B001's. His own statement that the two cases differ in kind and not in obvious strength fits my view, and I do not think the committee needs a rule that ranks methods below frameworks. I am not changing my configuration, but his point on validation is the strongest argument against it, and I count it as such.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson moved from Katz to Dorn and now proposes Autor, Dorn and Hanson, with the citation worded around technology and trade shocks to labour demand so that it does not claim priority for the task framework. She argues that a decade of replication and re-estimation shows maturity, not weakness.
responses.response: Her move to Autor, Dorn and Hanson removes the attribution instability I raised in round 1, and it matches the trio I proposed in my own opening. Her narrower wording also answers part of my concern about task-framework antecedents. B018 is therefore a more defensible package than the one I assessed in round 1, and I acknowledge that. I still do not move it above B001, for two reasons. The long-run size and persistence of the China-shock effects, and the shift-share identification, are still being actively revised, and I would rather wait for that to settle. A framework absorbed over three decades is also a more settled basis for a prize. I treat that as a difference of weighting that I could support in a later year, not as a rejection. B018 stays outside my two named alternatives only because I rank B003 and B050 closer, and she could fairly say the ordering is close.

responses.point: Dreber ranks B030 first because the firm-heterogeneity framework has been confronted with micro data more densely than protection-for-sale. She names the omission of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum as the main weakness and treats the Helpman overlap as a matter of which contribution is better established and more cleanly attributed.
responses.response: I agree with her rule for the Helpman overlap: choose on which contribution is better established and more cleanly attributed, and not on which has more votes. Applying it, I reach a different answer from hers. Her case on empirical confrontation is strong and I concede it. But she herself says the credit gap cannot be closed within three names without weakening the Melitz-Helpman core, and the contribution rests heavily on one 2003 paper. For B001 the credit is complete with two names. We differ on whether the denser empirical record of B030 outweighs its attribution gap. I find the gap harder to defend in a prize citation. I would not merge the two parts, since that would add a third name and blur the citations. A Grossman-Helpman award would also leave B030 open for later consideration.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B003 first. He would draft the citation on the intertemporal framework first and the exchange-rate puzzles second, accepting that the puzzles are an unresolved agenda with several originators and that the Redux sticky-price assumptions have limited empirical support. He separates the durable core from the vulnerable part.
responses.response: His response to my round-1 caution improves the case. If the citation rests on the intertemporal current-account framework and the microfounded welfare analysis, the main attribution problem with the puzzles drops out, and the two-name credit is clean. I keep B003 as my lead alternative, not my first choice, for two reasons. The distinctness from the Mundell-Fleming tradition is a real judgement call that I cannot settle from the files. The framework's durability also does not dispose of the question of how much of the Redux contribution survives its own price-setting assumptions. I would be comfortable voting for B003 if B001 does not hold, and I would want the citation worded as he describes.

responses.point: Teorell leads his B001 citation with organised interests and trade policy but also names the integration of innovation and growth into trade theory. He treats the growth strand as supporting, and he is unsure whether it overlaps with the 2025 prize.
responses.response: We agree on the laureates and on leading with political economy. I differ on his second clause. If the growth strand is only supporting, it adds little to the citation. If it is a co-equal basis for the prize, it brings the overlap issue and could look like two prizes merged into one, as he himself says. Neither of us can verify the 2025 prize from the files. So I would prefer the narrow citation, which depends on no uncheckable claim and which the ballot's stated discovery supports. I would not oppose the broader wording if a majority wants it. It would not change my vote.

uncertainties: How much the mixed empirical record of protection-for-sale should count against B001 relative to its influence on theory, estimation and trade-agreement analysis. I find it a limit but not disqualifying, and Krusell's view that it is more worrying is reasonable.

Whether the 2008 trade prize and the 2025 growth prize, as described by colleagues and not verified here, make a Grossman-Helpman award look insufficiently distinct. This matters mainly if the citation includes the growth strand, which is why I would keep it narrow.
Whether a majority would prefer to recognise trade through B030 because of its denser empirical record, and how an unresolved Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum gap would play against that.
Whether B018 with Autor, Dorn and Hanson is now stable enough that the persistence and shift-share debates, which I treat as an argument for waiting, would be judged resolved by other members.
Whether B003 or B050 should be my first fallback if B001 stalls. My ordering of the two is close and rests on general knowledge, without independent verification of citation or impact data.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. From the supplied profile I see no collaboration or institutional tie to Helpman or Grossman (B001) or to the credited names on my alternatives B003 (Obstfeld, Rogoff) and B050 (Moore, Kiyotaki, Gertler, Gilchrist). My listed collaborators in matching, kidney exchange and refugee placement include none of these names. My SSE affiliation alongside several committee colleagues is not a link to any candidate. My research in market design is distant from trade-policy theory. I disclose this without adjudicating it, and I note that the chair and several other members also prefer B001, which is a coincidence of views and not a tie on my side.
